questions.prompt: What three objects must all exist for a WMI event subscription to fire?
options: A service, a driver, and a registry key
__EventFilter (the trigger), an EventConsumer (the action), and __FilterToConsumerBinding (the link)
A scheduled task, a script, and a user account
questions.explanation: Without the binding linking filter to consumer, the other two objects are inert -- which is also why an orphaned filter or consumer is still evidence worth recording.

questions.prompt: Why does deleting the original dropper often fail to remove WMI subscription persistence?
options: The dropper reinstalls itself from the network
The payload can be embedded entirely inside the consumer as inline script or a command line, living in the WMI repository rather than in any file
WMI subscriptions cannot be deleted at all
The dropper is always stored in the registry as a backup
questions.explanation: When the code lives inside the consumer object in the WMI repository, there is no separate file to delete -- this is what makes it genuinely fileless persistence.

questions.prompt: Which Sysmon event IDs cover WMI subscription components?
questions.explanation: Sysmon 19 covers WmiEventFilter, 20 covers WmiEventConsumer, and 21 covers WmiEventConsumerToFilter -- seeing all three in sequence is a subscription being installed end to end.

questions.prompt: Why is 'does a WMI subscription exist' the wrong baseline question?
options: Legitimate management tooling like Configuration Manager and Intune uses them by design, so the real question is whether a given consumer is one of yours
questions.explanation: Because legitimate subscriptions are common in managed environments, the baseline is knowing what your management tooling registers so anomalies stand out against it.
